codex.worst_flaw: Auditing only credited visits leaves the pilot unable to detect whether technicians start uncredited jobs without completing the required safety checks.

claude.worst_flaw: The design randomises crews for a one-month pilot but never shows the number of crews is enough to detect a 10-point gain. It also ignores spillover between crews that share fixes and briefings, so the scale decision may rest on noise.

holistic.reason: Union-aware, fairness-focused design with audits, fallback, privacy and a randomised pilot is something I'd approve, but the dense credit rules and group-level 30-minute reward make it complex and weakly salient to technicians, and the lasting effect depends mainly on the app-friction fixes rather than the reward.

codex.worst_flaw: The scale-up rule sets a 10-point threshold without specifying the crew sample needed or how uncertainty in the adoption and safety estimates affects the decision.

claude.worst_flaw: The design gives no replayable event or policy versions and no shadow validation before launch, and it never checks whether paired-crew randomisation of about 300 technicians can detect the 10-point decision threshold or how much the programme costs.

holistic.reason: Strong safety guardrails, union co-design, privacy limits, randomised pilot and a stop rule make it approvable, but a crew-level €25 reward and a month of follow-up gives modest motivation and uncertain persistence unless the prefilled workflow fix does the real work.

claude.worst_flaw: The learning design randomises crews but never sets a feasible sample size, a way to handle uncertainty or spillover between crews, or a cost-per-lift threshold, and it judges durability on only a four-week follow-up, so the scale decision could rest on noise.

codex.worst_flaw: The safety audit samples only credited jobs, leaving unsafe starts on skipped or fallback jobs outside the programme’s pause rules and creating a launch blocker.

holistic.reason: Union-friendly design with team-level reward, no individual surveillance, safety-first handling of stop-work, and a randomized comparison earns approval, but the complexity of the credit rules, the reconciliation burden, and a reward of only 30 minutes of paid release time limit how strongly technicians will notice it and keep the habit once it ends.

claude.worst_flaw: The design judges success with a single-team before-and-after comparison. It never isolates what the reward adds beyond the routing and feedback changes, and it does not handle seasonality or case mix, so it cannot show incremental value.

codex.worst_flaw: The before-and-after pilot cannot isolate the effect of the paid hour from changes in workload, PR complexity, or engineers getting used to the new review queue.

holistic.reason: It is a rigorous, low-gimmick design with a diagnosis step, audit controls and a private-by-default reward that sceptical engineers should accept, but it is dense and operationally heavy, and a one-hour reward tied to an eight-hour deadline may be too weak a nudge to hold once rewards stop.

codex.worst_flaw: The pilot introduces better routing, private feedback, and a team reward together, so it cannot determine whether the reward adds enough value to justify its cost.

claude.worst_flaw: The evaluation is a single-team before/after comparison with no control or plain-support arm, so it cannot show whether the incentive adds anything beyond the routing and notification fixes, and the design admits it measures only the combined package.

holistic.reason: Rigorous, fair, privacy-conscious and sceptic-friendly, with diagnosis-first gating, audits and a reward-free follow-up, but it is complex to administer, the focus-time reward is modest, and habits may fade once the clock and reward end.

claude.worst_flaw: The design reaches its keep-and-extend decision from a single-team before-and-after comparison, with no concurrent comparison or way to separate the reward's effect from the queue, backup and protected time added at baseline. The design itself admits this only supports a feasibility decision.

codex.worst_flaw: The pilot lacks a comparison group receiving the same workflow support and private feedback, so it cannot establish whether the paid hour improves review timeliness.

holistic.reason: Unusually rigorous and sceptic-friendly (diagnosis first, fixes to blockers, audits, private data, a modest reward), but the paid hour reward is small and the workflow is dense, so engagement and post-reward persistence depend on the queue and backup fixes actually removing the delays.

codex.worst_flaw: Launch blocker: nurses could meet the reward and expansion thresholds by logging mainly during observed sessions, leaving routine kiosk adoption unverified.

claude.worst_flaw: The design only gives credit for kiosk entries matched to an observed action, so logging coverage is measured only while observers are present, where nurses already change their behaviour; with a plain before-and-after comparison and no comparison ward or condition, it cannot show what the reward adds over the kiosk support alone.

holistic.reason: Well-guarded on safety, privacy and gaming risks with a safe fallback, but the team-meal reward is weak, the logging credit is hard to reconcile through audit matching, and nurses have little reason to keep logging once the reward ends.

codex.worst_flaw: All three wards introduce the reward at the same time, so the pilot cannot distinguish its effect from growing kiosk familiarity, workflow fixes, or changes in the mix of cases observed.

claude.worst_flaw: The core reward metric ties ward credit to kiosk logging of observer-sampled actions, yet monthly observer audits are too sparse to yield a reliable per-ward matched rate (the n>=30 suppression may often block payout), and the before/after baseline with no concurrent comparison ward or plain-support arm cannot isolate the incentive's incremental value.

holistic.reason: The design is careful about safety, gaming and audit matching, but the reward is a modest catered break that depends on a complex ward-level matching rule. Nurses are unlikely to find that rule salient or motivating, and logging may fade once the reward ends.

claude.worst_flaw: The core measure is weak: kiosk logging adds no direct patient-safety value beyond observed compliance, and rewarding matches against observer audits encourages staff to log more while observers are present (a Hawthorne effect). The design also has no concurrent comparison ward, so it cannot show what the reward adds beyond plain workflow support.

codex.worst_flaw: The pilot has no concurrent plain-feedback comparison, and the kiosk layout changes before reward withdrawal, so the results cannot isolate the ward meal’s effect on adoption or persistence.

holistic.reason: Safety-first fallback, privacy protections, independent audit matching and pause rules are strong, but the 80% adoption threshold, matching burden and ward-meal reward make it complex, and gains likely fade once audit matching and rewards end.

codex.worst_flaw: The 30% target ignores differences in article availability and review turnaround, while rounding gives an agent with one eligible ticket a 100% personal target.

claude.worst_flaw: The design never deals with the CSAT bonus. Agents are pushed to link articles while their pay still depends on CSAT, and a 2-point CSAT drop is allowed. Nothing checks whether linked articles actually help customers, such as deflection or repeat contacts, so real value isn't separated from credit-farming. Missed and excused weeks (leave, outages) are also not handled clearly.

holistic.reason: Rigorous measurement, quality gates, and a randomized pilot are strong, but the reward is a modest 45 minutes of flex time for a team-level 30% target, the rules are dense, and the proposal never confirms agents will want to do this or that the workflow actually saves them effort, so interest and persistence are uncertain.

codex.worst_flaw: Only the reward arm gets weekly team progress posts, so the pilot cannot isolate the effect of protected paid time from the effect of team feedback.

claude.worst_flaw: The learning design is the weakest part: it randomises a few teams in a 60-person org with no power check, and it posts reward-arm team progress in the shared support channel where comparison teams can see it, so the comparison is likely underpowered and contaminated.

holistic.reason: Rigorous design with sound diagnosis, audit, quality guardrails and a randomized pilot, but the reward is a modest 30 minutes of team-level time with a 45% threshold, heavy admin and a seven-day verification delay dull its pull, and nothing builds habit or intrinsic value, so gains likely fade after rewards end.

codex.worst_flaw: The 40% target has no basis in measured feasibility, and rounding with a three-credit cap makes personal goals demand 100% adoption on a one-ticket week and less than 40% on a high-volume week, regardless of case mix.

claude.worst_flaw: The weekly goal of 40% of eligible volume, capped at three, is too low to track the target of an article on every resolved ticket, and comparing queues across a 60-person org has too few clusters to detect a 15-point gap, with no plan for uncertainty or spillover between queues.

holistic.reason: Unusually rigorous on measurement, gaming safeguards, CSAT protection and pilot design, but the worker-facing message is thin and a one-hour paid reward with weekly goals is modest, and article-search friction is only addressed late, so durability after rewards end is doubtful.
